fields.title: Disease Outbreak News: Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus, Democratic Republic of the Congo (28 August 2026)
fields.body:
**Situation at a glance**

Since the last Disease Outbreak News was published on 14 August 2026, the outbreak has spread from 54 to 60 health zones. The number of affected provinces stands at six out of 26 provinces of the country: Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, and Tshopo. Six additional health zones reported cases since the last update - Ganga and Viadana health zones in Bas-Uélé province, Biena, Manguredjipa, and Mutwanga in North Kivu, and Tshopo health zone in Tshopo province. As of 26 August 2026, a total of 5794 confirmed cases, including 2786 deaths, have been reported, corresponding to a crude case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.1%. These figures demonstrate a substantial increase in the scale and geographic extent of the outbreak over the past three months. The crude case fatality ratio of 48% underscores the severity of the disease and ongoing challenges related to timely case detection, access to and quality of clinical care, and effective interruption of viral transmission. Delays in recognizing cases increase the likelihood of onward transmission within households, communities and healthcare facilities. The outbreak remains a public health emergency of international concern, following the advice of Emergency Committee meeting convened on 18 August.

**Description of the situation**

Since the previous [Disease Outbreak News](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2026-DON615) was published on 14 August 2026, additional confirmed cases and deaths of BVD have been reported only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Cumulatively as of 26 August 2026, 5815 confirmed cases have been reported: 5794 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (including two cases diagnosed in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and subsequently treated in Germany), 20 in Uganda and one in France. A total of 2788 deaths have been reported, including two in Uganda. As of 26 August, at least 1314 patients have recovered, including 1293 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, 18 in Uganda, two in Germany and one in France.

As of 27 August, the 42-day enhanced monitoring period, as per international guidance, has been completed in both France and [Uganda](https://www.afro.who.int/countries/uganda/news/uganda-ends-ebola-outbreak-following-completion-42-day-countdown).

The continuing intensity of transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo means that the risk of further exportation across international borders remains. Entry and exit health screening and surveillance measures are in place at airports, ports and official land border crossings; however, movement through informal border crossing routes may occur, presenting an ongoing risk of virus exportation, importation and onward transmission. Therefore, cross‑border collaboration, and sustained surveillance and preparedness are essential to prevent further regional spread and ensure an effective public health response.

On 27 August, vaccination of health care workers using the Ervebo vaccine was initiated in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in some areas, including in Kisangani, Tshopo province. Although Ervebo is a safe vaccine, and effective against Ebola virus disease, it is not known whether it provides protection against the Bundibugyo virus in humans. Thus, starting a clinical trial of the vaccine, alongside this wider use, is key to provide important new evidence and inform future use of the vaccine.

The second IHR Emergency Committee meeting regarding the epidemic of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo took place on 18 August. Following the advice of the Committee, the Director-General agreed that the ongoing outbreak remains a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, and issued updated temporary recommendations to countries.

**Democratic Republic of the Congo**

Since 14 August 2026 when the last [Disease Outbreak News](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2026-DON615) was published, an additional 1129 confirmed cases, including 602 confirmed deaths, have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Although part of this increase likely reflects expanded surveillance, enhanced laboratory testing, improved diagnostic capacity, and periodic data backlog reconciliation, the sustained rise in number of cases and deaths are the result of continued transmission and substantial outbreak expansion. As of 26 August 2026, a total of 5794 confirmed cases, including 2786 deaths (CFR 48.1%), have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. To date, 1293 patients have recovered.

Cases have been reported from 60 health zones (HZ) across six provinces. Ituri has 28 health zones affected out of 36, followed by North Kivu (15/34), Haut-Uélé (6/13), Tshopo (7/23), South Kivu (1/34) and Bas Uélé (3/11). The most recently affected province, Bas-Uélé, started reporting cases since 12 August. The most recently affected health zones are Biena and Manguredjipa in North Kivu province. As of 26 August, of the 60 affected health zones, 81 new confirmed cases were reported in the last 24 hours from 19 health zones in Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uélé, and Tshopo provinces. Ituri remains the epicentre of the outbreak, with 4802 confirmed cases reported since the start of the outbreak, including 52 new confirmed cases reported in the last 24 hours, as of 26 August. Nord-Kivu is the second most affected province, with a cumulative number of 775 confirmed cases, including 22 reported in the last 24 hours, as of 26 August. The highest CFR (68%) in this outbreak has been reported from North Kivu province; the reasons for this high CFR are under investigation.

The number of individuals requiring contact monitoring has also increased substantially as the outbreak has expanded. As of 26 August, the proportion of contacts followed up in the last 24 hours is at 82.3% (22 091 seen out of 26 850 to follow up). The large number of contacts reflects the scale of potential exposure within affected communities.

The outbreak is unfolding in a conflict-affected humanitarian context marked by insecurity, armed violence, and large-scale displacement. More than 26 million people face acute food insecurity, and an estimated one million internally displaced people live in Ituri Province alone. Insecurity and displacement disrupt access to health care and essential services, restrict access for response teams, and impede surveillance, case investigation and contact follow-up. Overcrowding, limited water, sanitation and hygiene services, and restricted access to healthcare in mining communities, informal settlements and sites for internally displaced people further hinder early detection, infection prevention, and appropriate care. These conditions also make it harder to implement response measures consistently and to reach affected populations.

Between 18 May and 28 August 2026, enhanced public health intelligence conducted by WHO identified 76 Ebola-related signals across 23 countries and territories, supporting rapid verification, risk assessment and information sharing with national authorities through IHR National Focal Points. Most signals, 92% (70/76), including suspected cases among travellers and health-care workers and reports circulating in public sources, were subsequently ruled out through investigation and laboratory testing. The remaining six were confirmed as Ebola events.

**Epidemiology**

Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) is a severe Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, one of the *Orthoebolavirus* species. It is a zoonotic disease, with fruit bats suspected to be the natural reservoir.

Human infection is thought to occur through close contact with the blood or secretions of infected wildlife, such as bats or non-human primates, and it subsequently spreads from person-to-person through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces and materials. Transmission is particularly amplified in health-care settings when IPC measures are inadequate and during unsafe burial practices involving direct contact with deceased individuals.

The incubation period for BVD ranges from two to 21 days, and infected individuals are not infectious until symptom onset. Early symptoms such as fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, and sore throat are non-specific, which complicates clinical diagnosis and can delay detection. These symptoms then progress to gastrointestinal symptoms, organ dysfunction, and, in some cases, haemorrhagic manifestations.

CFRs in the past two BVD outbreaks, reported in Uganda and in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2007 and 2012, were 30% and 50%, respectively.

Differentiating BVD from other endemic febrile illnesses such as malaria is challenging without laboratory confirmation using PCR or antigen- or antibody-based assays. Outbreak control relies on rapid case identification, isolation and care, contact tracing, safe burials and strong community engagement, as no approved vaccines or specific treatments currently exist for BVD.

Since first detected in May 2026, this BVD outbreak has rapidly evolved into a large and geographically expanding epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with sustained transmission, high mortality and an increasing risk of further international spread. The current outbreak is the second documented Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the country, after the 2012 outbreak, and the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo irrespective of Ebola virus species. The population at greatest risk of exposure is concentrated in communities living in and moving through areas with active transmission.

**Public health response**

For detailed information about the ongoing public health response actions by the Ministry of Health, WHO and partners please refer to the latest situation reports published by the WHO Regional Office for Africa: [Ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo | WHO | Regional Office for Africa](https://www.afro.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease/outbreak-drc-26)

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in collaboration with WHO and partners, are continuing to implement and coordinate extensive public health measures, including disease surveillance, laboratory testing, infection prevention and control, clinical care, community engagement, research, logistics and support for response interventions and essential health services, engaging donors and mobilizing additional resources to address critical funding gaps and sustain response operations across affected and at-risk areas. A substantial scale-up is ongoing across all response pillars to get ahead of the outbreak.

**WHO risk assessment**

On 14 August 2026, WHO reassessed the risk of the outbreak of BVD to incorporate newly available information. The risk for countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo was separated from the risk for other countries in the African Region.

The risk in the Democratic Republic of the Congo was assessed as very high due to ongoing transmission and the continued expansion of the outbreak into new health zones, increasing the potential for further national and regional spread. The main considerations supporting this assessment include the substantial increase in the number of cases and considerable geographic extension of the outbreak since the previous risk assessment, and potential further increase in CFR as additional deaths are investigated and outcomes are established. In addition, reported transmission among healthcare workers, ongoing conflict and insecurity, laboratory capacity constraints, and absence of licensed vaccine or specific antiviral treatment were also considered as factors maintaining the very high risk.

The risk for countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo was again assessed as high due to sustained population mobility linked to cross-border trade and mining activities, variation in capacities and experience of BVD response, and variable levels of readiness. Uganda, the Central African Republic and South Sudan are of particular concern for importation given their proximity, high population mobility and connectivity with areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo currently experiencing intense transmission. For the Central African Republic and South Sudan, these risks are further compounded by high humanitarian needs, population displacement, insecurity and underlying limitations in health-system capacity.

The risk for the rest of the African region and at the global level was again assessed as low.

For further information, please see [WHO Rapid Risk Assessment-Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus, Democratic Republic of the Congo v4](https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/who-rapid-risk-assessment-ebola-disease-caused-by-bundibugyo-virus--democratic-republic-of-the-congo-v4)

**WHO advice**

Based on the currently available information, WHO advises against any restriction of travel to, or trade with, affected countries. WHO continues to closely monitor and, where necessary, verify travel and trade measures in relation to this event.

The updated [Temporary Recommendations](https://www.who.int/news/item/24-08-2026-second-meeting-of-the-ihr-emergency-committee-on-the-epidemic-of-ebola-bundibugyo-virus-disease-in-the-democratic-republic-of-the-congo-temporary-recommendations) issued to States Parties on 24 August 2026 underscore the importance of coordinated outbreak control, strengthened cross‑border collaboration, and sustained surveillance and preparedness to prevent further regional spread and ensure an effective public health response. Rapid recognition of cases, testing and optimized supportive care can reduce mortality, and improve community perceptions and acceptance of health care within the response.

On 7 August, the WHO Technical Advisory Group on candidate vaccine prioritization released a report regarding possible candidate vaccines for Bundibugyo virus disease. The members recommended that Ervebo, the only licensed Ebola vaccine (previously known as ebolavirus Zaire), be prioritized for inclusion in a randomized clinical trial in the context of the ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

In addition, WHO is sponsoring a clinical trial to find effective treatments against BVD. The trial began enrollment on 2 July. The trial, known as the PARTNERS trial, is now open in three different clinical management facilities in Ituri province and has enrolled over 250 people who are confirmed cases.

fields.title: Media resilience and risk communication take centre stage at Lake Chad Basin
fields.body:
N'Djamena, Chad – 29 July 2026 – As climate change, disasters and protracted crises increasingly converge across the Lake Chad Basin, strengthening the capacity of media to communicate risk and support early action has become an essential component of disaster risk reduction. Journalists, editors, disaster management authorities, United Nations agencies and regional partners gathered in N'Djamena from 27–29 July for a regional workshop aimed at strengthening climate reporting and media resilience across one of Africa's most vulnerable regions.

The workshop, organized by UNESCO in partnership with the African Union of Broadcasting (AUB) and hosted by Chad's Office National des Médias Audiovisuels (ONAMA) under the patronage of the Government of Chad, brought together media professionals from Cameroon, Chad, Niger and Nigeria. The event forms part of a regional initiative supporting media institutions to strengthen climate and disaster reporting, develop institutional disaster preparedness and response plans, and expand cross-border collaboration on issues affecting communities across the Lake Chad Basin.

## Reliable information for a region facing complex risks

Home to more than 30 million people, the Lake Chad Basin faces recurring droughts, floods, land degradation, climate variability and environmental change, while many communities continue to experience conflict, displacement and food insecurity. In these complex and fragile contexts, reliable public information plays a critical role in helping people understand risks, prepare for hazards and make informed decisions before disasters strike.

Throughout the three-day workshop, participants refined disaster preparedness and response plans for their media organizations, reviewed collaborative climate reporting projects, and exchanged practical experiences on solutions-oriented journalism, digital tools, artificial intelligence and reporting in fragile and conflict-affected environments. A field visit at the Lake Chad, peer learning and practical exercises helped journalists translate technical information into stories that are relevant, accessible and actionable for local audiences.

## From forecasts to life-saving journalism

A dedicated session led by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) focused on Early Warning Systems and Risk Communication: Journalism that Saves Lives, equipping participants with practical tools to transform scientific forecasts into clear, accurate and actionable public information. Working in simulated newsroom teams, journalists responded to a fictional early warning bulletin by producing public alerts, radio scripts and social media messages under tight deadlines. Rather than simply repeating technical forecasts, participants were challenged to explain what the hazard meant for people, who was at risk, what actions should be taken, and why the information could be trusted. Through peer review and guided feedback, they refined their reporting using core principles of effective warning messages, including clarity, relevance, urgency and actionable advice.

## Understanding what drives early action

Building on this exercise, UNDRR introduced a second scenario that shifted the focus from information delivery to human behaviour. Participants explored why communities sometimes fail to act despite receiving timely warnings, identifying barriers such as mistrust, previous false alarms, social norms, gender dynamics, fear of looting, limited resources and uncertainty about evacuation options.

The discussions highlighted that effective risk communication is not only about transmitting information but also about understanding the realities that shape people's decisions. By developing editorial angles that addressed these barriers—from explaining why a warning is different to providing practical guidance on where to go and what to do—journalists explored how reporting can strengthen trust, encourage early action and support a culture of preparedness. The exercises reinforced a central principle of people-centred early warning systems: warnings save lives only when they lead to informed action.

## Strengthening media resilience across borders

This workshop is part of UNDRR’s efforts to strengthen media’s approach to disaster coverage amid growing recognition that media institutions are themselves critical actors in disaster preparedness.

**Resources**

*Risk Media hub*

[Visit this toolkit ](https://www.preventionweb.net/hubs/risk-media-hub)for news media professionals reporting on disasters and resilience*Covering disaster from a different lens*

[Take this course](https://www.sparkblue.org/group/covering-disasters-different-lens/about) to build the skills needed for coverage that goes beyond immediate impacts and put the spotlight on underlying risks, vulnerability, and opportunities for reducing future disaster losses.

As climate-related hazards continue to intensify across the Lake Chad Basin, investing in media resilience and effective risk communication will remain essential for supporting informed decision-making, strengthening preparedness and advancing resilience in vulnerable communities.

**Democratic Republic of the Congo**

Since 14 August 2026 when the last [Disease Outbreak News](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2026-DON615) was published, an additional 1129 confirmed cases, including 602 confirmed deaths, have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Although part of this increase likely reflects expanded surveillance, enhanced laboratory testing, improved diagnostic capacity, and periodic data backlog reconciliation, the sustained rise in number of cases and deaths are the result of continued transmission and substantial outbreak expansion. As of 26 August 2026, a total of 5794 confirmed cases, including 2786 deaths (CFR 48.1%), have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. To date, 1293 patients have recovered.

Cases have been reported from 60 health zones (HZ) across six provinces. Ituri has 28 health zones affected out of 36, followed by North Kivu (15/34), Haut-Uélé (6/13), Tshopo (7/23), South Kivu (1/34) and Bas Uélé (3/11). The most recently affected province, Bas-Uélé, started reporting cases since 12 August. The most recently affected health zones are Biena and Manguredjipa in North Kivu province. As of 26 August, of the 60 affected health zones, 81 new confirmed cases were reported in the last 24 hours from 19 health zones in Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uélé, and Tshopo provinces. Ituri remains the epicentre of the outbreak, with 4802 confirmed cases reported since the start of the outbreak, including 52 new confirmed cases reported in the last 24 hours, as of 26 August. Nord-Kivu is the second most affected province, with a cumulative number of 775 confirmed cases, including 22 reported in the last 24 hours, as of 26 August. The highest CFR (68%) in this outbreak has been reported from North Kivu province; the reasons for this high CFR are under investigation.

The number of individuals requiring contact monitoring has also increased substantially as the outbreak has expanded. As of 26 August, the proportion of contacts followed up in the last 24 hours is at 82.3% (22 091 seen out of 26 850 to follow up). The large number of contacts reflects the scale of potential exposure within affected communities.

The outbreak is unfolding in a conflict-affected humanitarian context marked by insecurity, armed violence, and large-scale displacement. More than 26 million people face acute food insecurity, and an estimated one million internally displaced people live in Ituri Province alone. Insecurity and displacement disrupt access to health care and essential services, restrict access for response teams, and impede surveillance, case investigation and contact follow-up. Overcrowding, limited water, sanitation and hygiene services, and restricted access to healthcare in mining communities, informal settlements and sites for internally displaced people further hinder early detection, infection prevention, and appropriate care. These conditions also make it harder to implement response measures consistently and to reach affected populations.

**Figure 2: Number of confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, by date of notification, as of 26 August 2026**

**Figure 3: Number of deaths among confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo by date of notification, as of 26 August 2026**

Between 18 May and 28 August 2026, enhanced public health intelligence conducted by WHO identified 76 Ebola-related signals across 23 countries and territories, supporting rapid verification, risk assessment and information sharing with national authorities through IHR National Focal Points. Most signals, 92% (70/76), including suspected cases among travellers and health-care workers and reports circulating in public sources, were subsequently ruled out through investigation and laboratory testing. The remaining six were confirmed as Ebola events.

Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) is a severe Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, one of the *Orthoebolavirus* species. It is a zoonotic disease, with fruit bats suspected to be the natural reservoir.

Human infection is thought to occur through close contact with the blood or secretions of infected wildlife, such as bats or non-human primates, and it subsequently spreads from person-to-person through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces and materials. Transmission is particularly amplified in health-care settings when IPC measures are inadequate and during unsafe burial practices involving direct contact with deceased individuals.

The incubation period for BVD ranges from two to 21 days, and infected individuals are not infectious until symptom onset. Early symptoms such as fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, and sore throat are non-specific, which complicates clinical diagnosis and can delay detection. These symptoms then progress to gastrointestinal symptoms, organ dysfunction, and, in some cases, haemorrhagic manifestations.

CFRs in the past two BVD outbreaks, reported in Uganda and in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2007 and 2012, were 30% and 50%, respectively.

Differentiating BVD from other endemic febrile illnesses such as malaria is challenging without laboratory confirmation using PCR or antigen- or antibody-based assays. Outbreak control relies on rapid case identification, isolation and care, contact tracing, safe burials and strong community engagement, as no approved vaccines or specific treatments currently exist for BVD.

Since first detected in May 2026, this BVD outbreak has rapidly evolved into a large and geographically expanding epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with sustained transmission, high mortality and an increasing risk of further international spread. The current outbreak is the second documented Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the country, after the 2012 outbreak, and the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo irrespective of Ebola virus species. The population at greatest risk of exposure is concentrated in communities living in and moving through areas with active transmission.

For detailed information about the ongoing public health response actions by the Ministry of Health, WHO and partners please refer to the latest situation reports published by the WHO Regional Office for Africa: [Ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo | WHO | Regional Office for Africa](https://www.afro.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease/outbreak-drc-26)

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in collaboration with WHO and partners, are continuing to implement and coordinate extensive public health measures, including disease surveillance, laboratory testing, infection prevention and control, clinical care, community engagement, research, logistics and support for response interventions and essential health services, engaging donors and mobilizing additional resources to address critical funding gaps and sustain response operations across affected and at-risk areas. A substantial scale-up is ongoing across all response pillars to get ahead of the outbreak.

On 14 August 2026, WHO reassessed the risk of the outbreak of BVD to incorporate newly available information. The risk for countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo was separated from the risk for other countries in the African Region.

The risk in the Democratic Republic of the Congo was assessed as very high due to ongoing transmission and the continued expansion of the outbreak into new health zones, increasing the potential for further national and regional spread. The main considerations supporting this assessment include the substantial increase in the number of cases and considerable geographic extension of the outbreak since the previous risk assessment, and potential further increase in CFR as additional deaths are investigated and outcomes are established. In addition, reported transmission among healthcare workers, ongoing conflict and insecurity, laboratory capacity constraints, and absence of licensed vaccine or specific antiviral treatment were also considered as factors maintaining the very high risk.

The risk for countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo was again assessed as high due to sustained population mobility linked to cross-border trade and mining activities, variation in capacities and experience of BVD response, and variable levels of readiness. Uganda, the Central African Republic and South Sudan are of particular concern for importation given their proximity, high population mobility and connectivity with areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo currently experiencing intense transmission. For the Central African Republic and South Sudan, these risks are further compounded by high humanitarian needs, population displacement, insecurity and underlying limitations in health-system capacity.

The risk for the rest of the African region and at the global level was again assessed as low.

Based on the currently available information, WHO advises against any restriction of travel to, or trade with, affected countries. WHO continues to closely monitor and, where necessary, verify travel and trade measures in relation to this event.

The updated [Temporary Recommendations](https://www.who.int/news/item/24-08-2026-second-meeting-of-the-ihr-emergency-committee-on-the-epidemic-of-ebola-bundibugyo-virus-disease-in-the-democratic-republic-of-the-congo-temporary-recommendations) issued to States Parties on 24 August 2026 underscore the importance of coordinated outbreak control, strengthened cross‑border collaboration, and sustained surveillance and preparedness to prevent further regional spread and ensure an effective public health response. Rapid recognition of cases, testing and optimized supportive care can reduce mortality, and improve community perceptions and acceptance of health care within the response.

On 7 August, the WHO Technical Advisory Group on candidate vaccine prioritization released a report regarding possible candidate vaccines for Bundibugyo virus disease. The members recommended that Ervebo, the only licensed Ebola vaccine (previously known as ebolavirus Zaire), be prioritized for inclusion in a randomized clinical trial in the context of the ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

In addition, WHO is sponsoring a clinical trial to find effective treatments against BVD. The trial began enrollment on 2 July. The trial, known as the PARTNERS trial, is now open in three different clinical management facilities in Ituri province and has enrolled over 250 people who are confirmed cases.

fields.body:
Highlights

● Uganda declared the end of the outbreak on 28 July 2026 following the end of the mandatory 42-day monitoring period.

● The outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) threatens maternal health outcomes for an estimated 63,700 pregnant women living in affected areas. 1 Service disruptions and declining public confidence are leading women to avoid health facilities. Data from Ituri—the epicentre of the outbreak—shows a 65% rise in maternal deaths in the past ten weeks compared to the ten weeks prior. At the same time, contraceptive uptake has declined sharply, with use of short-acting oral contraceptive pills falling by 62.5% and injectable contraceptives by 54.3%. 2 This is particularly concerning in an area with over 360,000 women of childbearing age, where access to contraception plays a critical role in enabling women to avoid unintended pregnancies at a time when pregnancy carries heightened risks.

● In the DRC, UNFPA has strengthened its focus on ensuring the continuity of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and gender-based violence (GBV) services. To address the rising incidence of maternal deaths observed in the affected zones, UNFPA is working closely with partners to scale up risk communications and community engagement (RCCE) and improve the quality of care for pregnant mothers.

fields.title: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 15 (17-23 August 2026)
fields.body:
**SITUATION OVERVIEW**

According to the World Health Organization, as of 22 August 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 5,514 confirmed cases and 198 suspected cases of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease (BVD), with a case fatality ratio of 48 per cent and 1,200 recoveries. The outbreak remains a significant public health concern due to continued transmission in affected areas. The evolving outbreak continues to unfold in a complex humanitarian context characterized by population displacement, insecurity and constrained access to health services in affected areas. Continued armed-group activity and localized security incidents in parts of Ituri Province pose operational challenges for response activities, underscoring the need for sustained access, coordination and risk mitigation measures to support implementation of critical public health interventions. These challenges, coupled with ongoing transmission across multiple provinces, reinforce the importance of sustained investments in disease surveillance, early detection, infection prevention and control (IPC), community engagement and case referral systems to support timely response measures and reduce the risk of further spread. Population mobility and cross-border movements remain key considerations for outbreak preparedness and response efforts. During the reporting period, neighbouring countries continued to strengthen preparedness measures through disease surveillance, health screening, population mobility mapping, risk communication and community engagement (RCCE), cross-border coordination and capacity-building activities. These efforts support early detection and preparedness in areas at heightened risk of crossborder disease transmission. In the DRC, surveillance and mobility monitoring activities continued to support early detection and inform preparedness and response efforts in outbreak-affected areas. In line with the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) systemwide scale-up activation for infectious disease events, IOM continues to support outbreak response activities in Priority 1 countries, DRC and Uganda, while strengthening preparedness and readiness measures in neighbouring and at-risk countries.

fields.title: MSF opens new Ebola Treatment Centre in Beni, DRC
fields.body:
28 August 2026 - In response to the spread of the 17th Ebola disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is strengthening its response in North Kivu. In cooperation with the Ministry of Health, the organisation has opened a new Ebola Treatment Centre (ETC) in Beni. This new facility enables the rapid treatment of patients, strengthens contact tracing and supports the health authorities in their efforts to contain the spread of the virus. ​ ​

Declared on 15 May, this 17th outbreak has now spread to six provinces: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Bas-Uélé and Tshopo. As of 22 August, the country has recorded more than 5,514 confirmed cases and 2,642 confirmed deaths, this epidemic is now the largest Ebola disease outbreak in the DRC on record, and the fastest spreading ever recorded globally. While most confirmed cases are recorded in Ituri, the towns of Beni and Butembo in North Kivu account for a significant proportion of infections. In the province, 714 confirmed cases and 490 deaths were recorded until 22 August. ​ ​

In North Kivu, MSF is already supporting the health authorities through an ETC and isolation centres in Butembo. The opening of the new ETC in Beni further strengthens these capacities, enabling a faster response in one of the hardest-hit areas. ​ ​

“Every hour counts in the fight against Ebola disease. Early diagnosis and treatment as soon as the first symptoms appear significantly increase people’s chances of survival, whilst reducing the risk of transmission within families and communities,” says Albert Stern, MSF emergency coordinator. ​ ​

But the fight against Ebola disease is not confined to treatment centres, and it should not be done at the expense of other healthcare services. Albert Stern explains: “Ebola disease is terrifying, and many people refrain from seeking healthcare out of fear to catch the virus in the health facilities or due to false rumours about the care that is provided there. This means that patients who have diseases like malaria, which is the leading cause of death in the country, or women and girls who are pregnant, might not get the care they need. This risks causing more people getting sick or dying from other causes than Ebola disease. Therefore, working alongside local communities, MSF is also strengthening primary healthcare services in the affected areas.” ​

In Beni, free consultations for common illnesses and medical care are available at the four health care centres of Kanzulinzuli, Malepe, Madrandele and Kasabinyole. Eighteen isolation rooms are currently operational, with five additional rooms under construction in Kasabinyole. These facilities enable patients with malaria, respiratory infections and diarrhoea – or those showing symptoms consistent with Ebola disease – to be admitted quickly, isolated in dignified conditions, and provided with care and appropriate nutrition, whilst maintaining contact with their loved ones in accordance with preventive measures. This approach helps to limit the transmission of the virus whilst ensuring that patients receive compassionate care. ​

As pregnant women and girls are at high risk of complications during Ebola disease outbreaks, MSF is supporting sexual and reproductive healthcare and working to make childbirth safer across all the health centres we support in Beni. ​ ​

At the same time, MSF is developing a community-based response that works as closely as possible with local communities. In collaboration with local leaders, community representatives and civil society organisations, MSF teams are building awareness within communities, promoting acceptance of public health measures and facilitating the early identification of sick people so that they can be referred swiftly to healthcare facilities. ​ ​

Through this approach, which combines medical care, strengthening primary healthcare and community engagement, MSF is continuing to support health authorities in North Kivu to curb the spread of the virus and save as many lives as possible. ​ ​

Le premier semestre 2026 a confirmé la persistance des crises humanitaires au Tchad, poursuite des arrivées de réfugiés et de retournés du Soudan, persistance de l’insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle, exacerbation des aléas climatiques et tensions communautaires. S'y ajoutent les déplacements préventifs dans la province du Lac et l'épidémie de choléra déclarée depuis 13 juin dans le Hadjer-Lamis, puis N'Djamena et le Lac. Malgré un financement fortement contraint, les acteurs humanitaires ont maintenu et adapté leur réponse.  
 A titre de rappel, en 2026, 4,5 millions de personnes ont besoin d'une assistance humanitaire. Parmi elles, le HNRP 2026 cible 3,4 millions de personnes, dont 1,9 million ont été retenues dans le cadre de l'exercice de repriorisation. En comparaison à la même période de 2025, la progression est nette, le plan n'était financé qu'à 17% pour 23% de personnes couvertes. fields.title: Chad, Lac province: Handover of the Dar Es Salam health centre in Baga Sola marks a new step towards the integration of refugees into the national health system
fields.body:
**Baga Sola, 4 August 2026** – After ten years of support from UNHCR, the Dar Es Salam Health Centre in Lac province has been officially handed over to the Chadian health authorities.

Built in 2016 to meet the healthcare needs of Nigerian refugees who had arrived in Lac province following attacks by non-state armed groups (NSAGs), the centre has, over the years, become an essential local service for refugees, internally displaced people and host communities. It provides, among other services, general medical consultations, antenatal care, vaccinations, and nutritional support.

Since arriving in Dar Es Salam in 2014, Kaltouma Hassane, a Nigerian refugee, has relied on the health centre as a trusted source of care for her family. The facility supported her children from their earliest years through regular consultations, preventive services, and monitoring of their growth and development. She still visits the centre today and values the quality of care it provides to the community.

“I gave birth to two children there under good conditions. Since their birth, they have received regular check-ups for vaccinations and nutrition. This centre plays a major role in looking after the health of my whole family” she says.

The centre now serves more than 18,000 refugees, 6,900 internally displaced people and around 7,000 members of host communities, as well as residents of nearly 33 surrounding villages. In 2025 alone, the centre carried out 341 deliveries assisted by qualified healthcare staff, resulting in 377 live births; provided 17,973 general medical consultations; and treated 518 children suffering from severe acute malnutrition and 289 people with mental health conditions.

Following the handover, the health authorities are now responsible for managing the centre. The healthcare staff (12 staff members) have been retained, and the supply of medicines will now be channelled through the Provincial Supply Pharmacy rather than being provided by UNHCR. The Health Centre Management Committee and the Health Committee are also involved in supporting the centre’s management and mobilising the community.

For Dr Sam Koulmini, the Health Ministry’s Provincial Delegate for Lac province, this handover goes beyond the management of a single centre. “This handover is a catalyst for the health system. It gives a significant boost to the entire sector, particularly in the Baga Sola district,” he explains.

In fact, the integration process had already begun before the transfer. The refugees from Dar Es Salam are already included in the population data used by the health authorities and are considered in the planning of health activities. The centre itself is one of the 17 health centres in Baga Sola Health District and falls under the supervision of the Lac Provincial Health and Prevention Delegation of the Health Ministry.

“The refugees are already integrated and included in Chad’s population data. All activities are planned down to the smallest detail with them in mind” explains Dr Koulmini.

Since 2016, UNHCR has supported the centre's operations alongside the health authorities. This support has focused on health staff, medicines, equipment, medical referrals and capacity-building for staff and the Health Centre Management Committee.  
  
At the time of the handover, all the centre's infrastructure and equipment were transferred to the health authorities, along with a stock of medicines and medical supplies worth over 75,000,000 CFA francs (~$133,500). An amount of 2,899,500 CFA francs (~$5,160), generated through the cost-recovery mechanism, is also available to contribute to the centre's operational expenses. An ambulance ensures that medical referrals to Baga Sola and Bol can continue.  
  
For Abakar Mahamat, who has overseen the centre since July 2026, the priority is now to ensure that services continue without interruption. "Ensuring continuity depends on three things: the presence of healthcare staff, the availability of medicines, and the availability of the ambulance to facilitate referrals to Baga Sola or Bol," he explains. He is also counting on the Health Centre Management Committee and the Health Committee to support him in managing the centre.  
  
However, continuity of care will also depend on the resources available. A large proportion of the population served has low incomes, which could limit the revenue generated from cost-recovery. Yet this revenue is needed, in particular, to help replenish stocks of medicines and keep the centre running. Health authorities also identify energy as a challenge, as the generator requires fuel to operate.  
  
For Kaltouma Hassane, these issues boil down to very practical concerns. "For the centre's future, it is essential that medicines continue to be available and that healthcare staff remain in place to ensure quality care for the population."  
  
UNHCR will remain committed after the handover, in particular through monitoring and advocacy where necessary. For Miguel Urquia, Head of the UNHCR office in Baga Sola, the work of the Health Centre Management Committee will be particularly important in monitoring the centre's management and alerting the authorities in the event of difficulties.  
  
"This is a major step towards inclusion in national systems" he emphasises. "Refugees will have the same access to healthcare as the local population, both now and in the future."

L’Indice des solutions et de la mobilité dans les zones de santé d’Angumu, Mahagi et Rimba, basé sur des données collectées du 3 au 23 juin 2026 dans le cadre d’un exercice autonome, met en évidence une stabilité globale modérément favorable, avec un score composite de 0,67 à travers 313 villages évalués. Si la majorité des communautés sont perçues comme stables et optimistes quant à leur avenir, d’importants défis persistent en matière d’accès aux services de base, de connectivité et de cohésion sociale.

Les résultats révèlent des disparités importantes entre les zones de santé : Rimba et Mahagi affichent les scores les plus élevés, tandis qu’Angumu demeure en retrait en raison de faiblesses liées aux conditions de vie, à la cohésion sociale et à l’accès aux services. Dans le contexte de l’épidémie d’Ebola en cours, le renforcement des infrastructures sanitaires, de la connectivité et des services essentiels reste indispensable pour soutenir des solutions durables et renforcer la résilience des communautés affectées par les déplacements.

fields.title: Regional External Update #39 West and Central Africa Region - Eastern DRC Situation - July 2026
fields.body:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Persistent conflict and insecurity continued to drive a deepening displacement crisis in eastern DRC, with new internal displacement still outpacing returns in several affected areas. Smaller but steady cross-border movements into neighbouring countries also accumulated to more than 16,400 new Congolese arrivals since January 2026, adding pressure on host communities and overstretched services.

• The Ebola outbreak further exposed the deadly overlap between insecurity, displacement and weak basic services in the DRC, with more than 5,600 confirmed cases and over 2,700 deaths1 , over three months after the outbreak was declared a public health emergency of international concern. Uganda however declared itself Ebola-free on 28 July, but cross-border preparedness remained critical. UNHCR continued contributing to the Government-led response in displacement settings despite significant funding challenges.

• Despite the volatile context, voluntary returns maintained momentum, supported by health screening, water, sanitation and hygiene measures and cross-border coordination. By 31 July, around 51,000 Congolese refugees had self-organized their return from Burundi and 14,200 Government-UNHCR facilitated returns to the DRC had been recorded since the beginning of the year.
